clue.text: Good-for-nothing given award rejected as site manager

indicators.note: one item is handed something which it then holds inside itself

parts.note: a waster is an idle, useless person

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so these letters run the other way

parts.note: the MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A layabout is handed an honour, which is turned down, and he ends up running a building site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Site' suggests a construction site, but the definition means a website. The MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: A webmaster is the person who runs and maintains a website, so a website administrator.

clue.text: Consumer of walnut perhaps solicited energy-less grub

indicators.note: less means without, so one letter is taken away

parts.note: solicited is WOOED (courted); drop E for energy
a grub is a worm-like larva

explanation.surface: Someone eyeing a walnut, perhaps the nut, is asked to eat bland food.
explanation.walkthrough: Walnut here is the timber, not the nut; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a wood that the larva bores into.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodworm is the larva of beetles that tunnels through and eats furniture timber such as walnut.

clue.text: Black reptile houses zoo originally used in storm

parts.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

indicators.note: to house something is to give it room inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a lizard is a reptile

indicators.note: originally points to the very start, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: first letter of zoo

explanation.surface: A dark reptile keeps a zoo running, which comes in handy during a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The inserted letter sits beside the reptile's own Z, which is why the answer has a double Z.
explanation.definitionFit: A blizzard is a severe snowstorm with high winds, a specific type of storm.

clue.text: Slowly American soldier supports girl with love

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever supports another sits below it, so it comes later

parts.note: Ada is a girl's name
GI is a US soldier
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A US soldier gradually comes to support a girl he loves.
explanation.walkthrough: GI is the standard nickname for an American private soldier; adagio is a tempo marking in music.
explanation.definitionFit: Adagio is the Italian musical tempo marking meaning at a slow, leisurely pace.

clue.text: Difficult test involves detective losing diamonds

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap up within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a try is an attempt or test

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter goes

parts.note: dick is old slang for a private detective
D is the abbreviation for the diamonds suit in cards; this letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A hard exam is set featuring a detective who has lost some jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick is old slang for a private detective. D is the bridge abbreviation for the diamonds suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Tricky describes something hard to handle or requiring care, a close synonym of hard.

clue.text: Pardon that is pre-empting nothing in censure

indicators.note: to pre-empt is to take something's place first, so one piece replaces another

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
nothing is zero, O
to reprove is to censure

explanation.surface: A pardon that comes before any criticism at all is handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: The O in REPROVE is swapped out for IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprieve cancels or postpones a punishment, which is what a pardon does too.

clue.text: Second pound daughter wasted getting second-class firework

indicators.note: something wasted is lost or thrown away, so a letter disappears

parts.note: S abbreviates second
QUID is slang for a pound; drop D for daughter
B is a second grade, as in B-list

explanation.surface: A second pound is squandered by a daughter on a cheap firework.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for one pound sterling. A damp squib is the familiar phrase for a firework that fizzles out.
explanation.definitionFit: A squib is a small explosive firework that hisses before going bang.

clue.text: Apparently, pals begin to play?

parts.note: surface reading: seemingly, friends getting together
setter's reading: a synonym for hit, written upward in this down entry, spells pals
a band begins playing a tune

explanation.walkthrough: SLAP means strike; written up the grid it reads PALS, so the phrase cryptically describes pals. 'Apparently' flags this reverse-style trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike up a tune is to start playing it, used of bands and orchestras beginning music.

clue.text: Nancy's article absolutely biased

parts.note: Nancy is a French city, and un is the French indefinite article
just means absolutely, as in 'just perfect'

explanation.surface: Nancy wrote a newspaper piece that was thoroughly one-sided.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name, but it is a city in France, so her article is a French one.
explanation.definitionFit: Unjust means unfair, and a biased judgement is an unfair, prejudiced one.

clue.text: Saw six-footer introducing husband and lord

indicators.note: to introduce is to bring something into, so a piece is put inside

parts.note: an insect has six feet, and a bee is one
H abbreviates husband
LD abbreviates lord

explanation.surface: Someone saw a very tall person presenting a husband and a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it means a creature with six feet, an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, an old word for to see or look upon.

clue.text: Old friend seizes equipment for paper manipulation

indicators.note: to seize is to grab and hold, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: O abbreviates old
a rig is a set of equipment
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A longtime pal grabs the tools needed for handling paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old friend' reads as one phrase, but it splits in two, and the equipment goes between them. Ami is the French word for friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding sheets into shapes, a skilled handling of the material.

clue.text: Church singer in vulgar assurance

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: in places one thing within another

parts.note: rude means vulgar
a tit is a songbird

explanation.surface: A choir member is caught being crudely overconfident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' suggests a chorister, but it is a songbird; the tit is a small common bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Certitude is complete confidence or conviction, which is what assurance means here.

clue.text: Journal regularly ignored Conservative speech

indicators.note: skipping at an even interval leaves every other letter

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of journal
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A newspaper kept passing over a Tory politician's address.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Oratory is the art of public speaking, so eloquent formal speech.

clue.text: Pressed city promoting River Dee

indicators.note: to promote is to move up, so one letter shifts earlier in the word

parts.note: Exeter is a cathedral city in Devon
Dee is the spelling of the letter D
names the letter that moves: R abbreviates river, and Exeter's own R is moved up

explanation.surface: A city campaigns to publicise the River Dee.
explanation.walkthrough: The River Dee is real, but here R is moved up two places within EXETER and Dee is just the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert pressure is to press, so exerted works as the past tense, meaning applied force.

clue.text: Increase in mature corporation power studied after pre-Renaissance period

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed second, behind it

parts.note: the era before the Renaissance in Europe
P is the symbol for power
to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: A big company's growth in power is analysed against medieval history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a business, but it is an old jokey word for a paunch or pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-age spread is the weight people gain around the waist in their forties and fifties, expanding the belly.

clue.text: Allow this section of clues to become disappointments

parts.note: to let is to allow
the clue sits among the downs, one of the two sections of clues

explanation.surface: A solver lets a whole column of clues turn sour.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to itself: it is printed in the Down list.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-down is a failure to meet expectations, which is what a disappointment is.

clue.text: Robots do drains badly

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters end up in a jumbled order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Machines make a poor job of unblocking the plumbing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a complaint about robot plumbers; the clue's first word alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Androids are robots built in human form, a type of mechanical humanoid.

clue.text: Required target limiting associate employment at first

indicators.note: to limit is to set boundaries around, so outer letters hem in an inner piece

parts.note: an end is an aim or target
to associate is to join

indicators.note: at first points to the opening, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of employment

explanation.surface: A required goal restricted a partner's hiring in the early stages.
explanation.walkthrough: The target holds two pieces at once, the associate and the single initial letter, one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To enjoin is to order or instruct formally, so enjoined means commanded or made obligatory.

clue.text: Pair upset about morning reverie

indicators.note: something upset is overturned, and in a down entry that means turned upside down

parts.note: a dyad is a pair
re means about or concerning
AM abbreviates morning

explanation.surface: Two people are upset about a morning spent idly musing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal, but it is RE, as in a letter's subject line.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a state of pleasant dreamy absorption, which is a daydream.

clue.text: Worked up about copyright, left

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: exited means went out, left
C is the copyright symbol, as in ©

explanation.surface: Someone got angry over a copyright issue and walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is a verb here, not a direction; it wraps around the C.
explanation.definitionFit: To be worked up is to be agitated or emotionally aroused, a sense of excited.

clue.text: Obliterate European force going to front

parts.note: E abbreviates European
F is the physics symbol for force
the face is the front of something

explanation.surface: A European army advances to the battle line to wipe out the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front' sounds military, but it means a face, as in the face of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: To efface is to rub out or erase, making something disappear completely.

clue.text: Hint about level of intelligence for group

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a clue is a hint
IQ, intelligence quotient, measures intelligence

explanation.surface: A tip on how bright a team is.
explanation.walkthrough: A clue placed around IQ, fitting for a crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: A clique is a small exclusive circle of people, a kind of social group.

clue.text: Dismal starters of jam and yellowing bird

parts.note: blue means gloomy or sad

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only initial letters count

parts.note: first letters of jam, and, yellowing

explanation.surface: A gloomy picture of jam starting to go yellow beside a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' is part of the fodder, not a link: its A is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The blue jay is a crested North American songbird of the crow family.

clue.text: Broken sled discovered in ado

parts.note: bust means broken

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover stripped, so the outer letters go

parts.note: the middle of sled

explanation.surface: A smashed sledge is found amid a lot of fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as found, but splits as dis-covered: uncovered, losing its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado means fuss and busy activity, and bustle is energetic commotion.

clue.text: Losing head, drunk's crazy bringing in company to open bottle

indicators.note: a word without its head has its opening letter removed
to bring in is to take inside, so one piece is placed within
crazy means wild and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: drunk without its first letter
CO abbreviates company

explanation.surface: A drunk has lost his head and gone mad, getting friends to help open a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': the beheaded word is crazy, then takes in CO.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncork is to pull out the cork stopper, opening a wine bottle.

clue.text: Trifling 'solid of revolution' reconstructed in Toledo strangely vanishes

indicators.note: something reconstructed is rebuilt in a new form, so letters are rearranged
strangely means in an odd fashion, so the removed letters may come out in any order
what vanishes is gone, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; strangely says these letters leave in any order

explanation.surface: A petty geometry term is rebuilt in a Spanish city where it oddly disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of IN TOLEDO, scattered through the phrase, are removed; the nine left are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Frivolous means lacking serious purpose or value, so petty and trivial.

clue.text: Their hollow measure could be best?

indicators.note: something hollow has its inside emptied, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: outer letters of their
an ounce is a measure of weight

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a group's empty yardstick might be the finest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective but is the verb, to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce is to defeat heavily, and to best someone is to defeat them.

clue.text: Last of tourists moving to east in channel vessels

indicators.note: east is right on a map, so a letter shifts towards the end
last of takes only the final letter

parts.note: last letter of tourists, the letter to move
a sewer is a channel for waste; its opening S is the one moved

explanation.surface: The final group of sightseers heads east on cross-Channel boats.
explanation.walkthrough: The channel is SEWER; its S moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewers are large jugs or pitchers, which are containers for liquid.

clue.text: Tremble as some say ruin won't take over chief's territory

indicators.note: as some say points to a particular way of speaking the word

parts.note: sheikh is pronounced shake by some

indicators.note: refusing to take something means leaving it out

parts.note: doom is ruin
O abbreviates over in cricket scoring; this letter is dropped

explanation.surface: People quake at the prospect of disaster overtaking a leader's land.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheikh has two pronunciations, 'shake' and 'shayk', hence 'some'. An over is a set of six balls in cricket, abbreviated O.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheikhdom is the land ruled by a sheikh, an Arab leader or head of a tribe.
